lessons.title: Units, targets and the boot process

scenes.text: Sana restarted nginx, rebooted the VM, and nginx was down again.
Started ≠ enabled. systemd tracks both.

steps.title: Unit types
steps.body:
- `.service` daemons, `.socket` socket activation, `.timer` schedules, `.mount`/`.automount`, `.target` groups of units, `.path` file watchers
- Vendor units: `/usr/lib/systemd/system`; admin units/overrides: `/etc/systemd/system` (wins)
- Targets: `multi-user.target` (text, servers), `graphical.target`, `rescue.target`, `emergency.target`

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body: `systemctl get-default` → multi-user.target. `systemctl set-default graphical.target` changes the boot target. `systemctl isolate rescue.target` switches now.

steps.title: start vs enable
steps.body: `start` = now; `enable` = create symlinks so it starts at boot; `enable --now` does both. `mask` links to /dev/null so nothing can start it.

lessons.title: Lab: Write a custom service unit

scenes.text: Developers hand Sana a Flask app started with 'python3 app.py' in tmux.
She turns it into a supervised systemd service with restarts and a dedicated user.

steps.title: Minimal unit
steps.body:
```
[Unit]
Description=Orders API
After=network-online.target
Wants=network-online.target

[Service]
User=orders
WorkingDirectory=/opt/orders
ExecStart=/opt/orders/venv/bin/python app.py
Restart=on-failure
RestartSec=5
Environment=PORT=8081

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target
```

steps.title: Hardening extras
steps.body: `NoNewPrivileges=yes`, `ProtectSystem=full`, `PrivateTmp=yes`, `UMask=0027`, `MemoryMax=512M`. `systemd-analyze security orders` scores exposure.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Relative path in ExecStart (must be absolute)
- Forgetting daemon-reload
- Type=simple program that forks into background → systemd thinks it died; use Type=forking or run in foreground.

scenes.text: nginx logs 'Too many open files' under load.

steps.title: Drop-ins
steps.body:
`systemctl edit nginx` creates `/etc/systemd/system/nginx.service.d/override.conf`:
```
[Service]

```
- `systemctl cat nginx` shows the merged unit
- To replace a list setting like ExecStart, first clear it: `ExecStart=` then the new line
- `systemctl revert nginx` removes overrides

steps.title: Verify
steps.body: `systemctl show nginx -p LimitNOFILE` → LimitNOFILE=65536. Check a worker: `grep 'open files' /proc/$(pgrep -o nginx)/limits`.

steps.title: systemctl edit reloads for you
steps.body: It runs daemon-reload automatically after you save; you still need to restart the service.

lessons.title: Lab: Capstone · Journal forensics after a crash

scenes.text: db02 rebooted unexpectedly at 03:12. Was it the kernel, power, or a person?
Sana needs a persistent journal and good filters.

steps.title: journalctl filters
steps.body:
- `--list-boots`, `-b -1` previous boot
- `-p err` priority err and above (emerg, alert, crit, err, warning, notice, info, debug)
- `--since '2026-11-26 02:50' --until '03:15'`
- `-k` kernel messages, `-f` follow, `-o json-pretty`
- Persistence: `Storage=persistent` in /etc/systemd/journald.conf or create /var/log/journal

steps.title: Clues
steps.body: Kernel OOM: `Out of memory: Killed process`. Human: `systemd-logind: System is rebooting` + sudo entry. Hardware/power: previous boot log simply stops with no shutdown messages.

steps.title: Disk use
steps.body: `journalctl --disk-usage`; trim with `--vacuum-size=500M` or `SystemMaxUse=`.

lessons.title: Package families and how they work

scenes.text: Rohit's team runs Rocky Linux for apps and Ubuntu for CI runners.
He needs both toolchains in his head.

steps.title: Layers
steps.body:
| Task | RHEL family | Debian family |
- Low-level: `rpm` / `dpkg` (one local package, no dependency solving)
- High-level: `dnf` (yum) / `apt` (dependency solving, repos)
- Repo config: `/etc/yum.repos.d/*.repo` / `/etc/apt/sources.list.d/*` (newer Ubuntu: `.sources` files)
- Refresh metadata: dnf does it automatically / `apt update` required before install

steps.title: Same task both ways
steps.body:
- Install: `dnf install nginx` / `apt install nginx`
- Search: `dnf search nginx` / `apt search nginx`
- Info: `dnf info nginx` / `apt show nginx`
- Remove: `dnf remove x` / `apt remove x` (`apt purge` also removes config)
- Installed list: `rpm -qa` / `dpkg -l`

steps.title: Mixing tools
steps.body: Don't install random .rpm/.deb files with rpm -i/dpkg -i when a repo exists — you lose dependency handling and updates.

steps.title: Trust
steps.body:
Packages are signed; the repo's public key must be imported and `gpgcheck=1` set.

```
[internal-tools]
name=Contoso internal tools
baseurl=https://repo.contoso.local/el9/$basearch/
enabled=1
gpgcheck=1
gpgkey=https://repo.contoso.local/RPM-GPG-KEY-contoso
```

- `dnf repolist`, `dnf config-manager --set-disabled name`

steps.body: Modern apt uses a keyring per repo: `signed-by=/etc/apt/keyrings/vendor.gpg` in the source entry. `apt-key` is deprecated.

steps.title: Never gpgcheck=0 in production
steps.body: It lets anyone who can tamper with traffic or the mirror push code that runs as root.

courses.title: Scheduling: cron, at and systemd timers
courses.summary: Automate recurring work reliably: crontab syntax, environment pitfalls, one-off at jobs, systemd timers with OnCalendar and Persistent, and logging/alerting for scheduled jobs. Independent practice material; not affiliated with or endorsed by the exam provider. Check the official exam guide for the current skills outline.
outcomes: Learners can write and read crontab lines confidently
Learners can avoid PATH/environment and output pitfalls
Learners can create systemd timers with OnCalendar and Persistent

lessons.title: Lab: Crontab syntax drills

story.title: The report that ran every minute

scenes.text: Someone wrote '* 2 * * *' meaning 2 a.m. — it ran 60 times between 02:00 and 02:59.
Five fields, carefully.

steps.title: Five fields
steps.body:
`minute hour day-of-month month day-of-week command`

- `30 2 * * *` 02:30 daily
- `*/15 * * * *` every 15 minutes
- `0 9 * * 1-5` 09:00 Mon–Fri
- `0 0 1 * *` midnight on the 1st
- `@reboot`, `@daily` shortcuts
- `crontab -e` edit, `-l` list, `-u user` as root; system jobs in `/etc/cron.d/` include a **user** field

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
1. 'At 23:45 every Sunday' → `45 23 * * 0`.
2. 'Every 6 hours on the hour' → `0 */6 * * *` (00,06,12,18).
3. `0 2 * * *` — the fix for the 60-runs bug.

steps.title: DOM + DOW
steps.body: If both day-of-month and day-of-week are restricted, cron runs when **either** matches. `0 0 1 * 1` = 1st of month OR every Monday.

steps.title: Cron pitfalls
steps.body:
- Minimal environment: PATH often `/usr/bin:/bin` → use absolute paths or set `PATH=` in the crontab
- `%` is special in crontab (newline) → escape as `\%` e.g. `date +\%F`
- Output is mailed to the owner or lost → redirect `>> /var/log/job.log 2>&1`
- Logs of cron itself: `journalctl -u crond` (RHEL) / `-u cron` (Debian)

steps.title: Good line
steps.body:
`15 1 * * * /usr/local/bin/backup.sh >> /var/log/backup.log 2>&1`

Prevent overlaps: `flock -n /run/backup.lock /usr/local/bin/backup.sh`.

steps.title: Test in cron's environment
steps.body: `env -i /bin/sh -c '/usr/local/bin/backup.sh'` approximates the bare environment.

lessons.title: Lab: systemd timers

scenes.text: A laptop-class edge box is off at 02:00 and misses its cleanup every night.
A timer with Persistent=true catches up at boot.

steps.title: Timer + service pair
steps.body:
`cleanup.service` (Type=oneshot, ExecStart=…) and `cleanup.timer`:
```
[Timer]
OnCalendar=*-*-* 02:00:00
Persistent=true
RandomizedDelaySec=10min

[Install]
WantedBy=timers.target
```
- Enable the **timer**: `systemctl enable --now cleanup.timer`
- `systemctl list-timers` next/last run
- `systemd-analyze calendar 'Mon..Fri 18:00'` validates expressions

steps.title: OnCalendar examples
steps.body:
- `daily` = `*-*-* 00:00:00`
- `Mon..Fri *-*-* 09:00`
- `*-*-01 03:00` 1st of month
- `*:0/15` every 15 minutes
- Monotonic: `OnBootSec=5min`, `OnUnitActiveSec=1h`

steps.title: Why timers
steps.body: Logs in the journal per run, dependencies, resource controls, catch-up with Persistent, no overlap (the service won't start twice while active).

lessons.title: Modes, contexts and type enforcement

scenes.text: A forum post tells Zoya to disable SELinux to fix a 403.
Her senior says: 'Understand the label, fix the label.'

steps.title: Concepts
steps.body:
- Modes: **enforcing** (deny + log), **permissive** (log only), **disabled**
- `getenforce`, `setenforce 0|1` (runtime), `/etc/selinux/config` (boot)
- Every process and file has a context `user:role:type:level`, e.g. `system_u:object_r:httpd_sys_content_t:s0`
- **Type enforcement**: policy says which process types (domains like `httpd_t`) may access which file/port types

steps.title: See labels
steps.body: `ls -Z /var/www/html` → `httpd_sys_content_t`. `ps -eZ | grep httpd` → `system_u:system_r:httpd_t:s0`. Files in /home are `user_home_t` — httpd_t can't read them.

steps.title: Why not disable
steps.body: SELinux contains a compromised service. Disabling it removes a major barrier. Switching from disabled back to enforcing needs a full relabel.

lessons.title: Lab: Diagnose an AVC denial

scenes.text: Zoya moved a site from /home/zoya/site to /var/www/shop with mv. Apache returns 403.

steps.title: Finding denials
steps.body:
- `ausearch -m AVC -ts recent`
- `journalctl -t setroubleshoot` (if setroubleshoot installed) — plain-English advice
- `sealert -a /var/log/audit/audit.log`
- Raw: `grep denied /var/log/audit/audit.log`

steps.title: Reading one
steps.body:
`avc: denied { read } for pid=2211 comm="httpd" name="index.html" scontext=system_u:system_r:httpd_t:s0 tcontext=unconfined_u:object_r:user_home_t:s0 tclass=file permissive=0`

→ httpd_t tried to read a user_home_t file. **mv keeps the old label**; cp creates a new label from the destination.

steps.title: Quick fix vs right fix
steps.body: `restorecon -Rv /var/www/shop` resets labels to the policy default for that path — correct here because /var/www already maps to httpd_sys_content_t.

steps.title: Map
steps.body:
- journald: everything from systemd units (`journalctl`)
- `/var/log/messages` (RHEL) or `/var/log/syslog` (Debian) — general syslog
- `/var/log/secure` (RHEL) / `/var/log/auth.log` (Debian) — authentication, sudo

- `/var/log/dnf.log` / `/var/log/apt/history.log` — package changes
- App logs: `/var/log/nginx/`, `/var/log/mariadb/`, app-specific dirs
- `dmesg` / `journalctl -k` — kernel ring buffer (disks, OOM, NIC)

steps.title: Symptom → log

lessons.title: Lab: logrotate

scenes.text: app.log grew to 38 GB because no rotation was configured.
Dev writes a logrotate rule.

steps.title: logrotate rule
steps.body:
`/etc/logrotate.d/orders`:
```
/var/log/orders/*.log {
    daily
    rotate 14
    compress
    delaycompress
    missingok
    notifempty
    create 0640 orders orders
    postrotate
        systemctl kill -s HUP orders.service
    endscript
}
```
- Runs daily via a systemd timer (logrotate.timer) or cron.daily
- `copytruncate` for apps that can't reopen logs (small risk of losing lines)

steps.title: Test
steps.body: `logrotate -d /etc/logrotate.d/orders` debug (dry run). `logrotate -f /etc/logrotate.d/orders` force now.

lessons.title: Block devices and naming

scenes.text: The cloud team attached a new disk to db04. Where is it?

steps.title: Naming
steps.body:
- SCSI/SATA/virtio-scsi: `/dev/sda`, partitions `/dev/sda1`
- virtio-blk: `/dev/vda`
- NVMe: `/dev/nvme0n1`, partitions `/dev/nvme0n1p1`
- Stable names: `/dev/disk/by-uuid/`, `by-id/`, `by-path/`
- Tools: `lsblk -f`, `blkid`, `fdisk -l`, `dmesg | tail`

steps.title: GPT vs MBR
steps.body:
- **MBR**: max 2 TiB per disk (with 512-byte sectors), 4 primary partitions (or extended)
- **GPT**: huge disks, 128 partitions by default, backup header at the end, required for UEFI boot

steps.title: Solved example

lessons.title: LVM concepts

scenes.text: Fixed partitions keep filling. Lakshmi wants volumes she can grow without downtime.
LVM pools disks into volume groups.

steps.title: Layers
steps.body:
- **PV** physical volume: a disk or partition (`pvcreate`)
- **VG** volume group: pool of PVs, carved into **extents** (default 4 MiB)
- **LV** logical volume: block device from VG extents → `/dev/vg/lv` = `/dev/mapper/vg-lv`
- Views: `pvs`, `vgs`, `lvs` (short), `pvdisplay`… (long)

steps.title: Extent maths
steps.body: VG of 2 × 50 GiB PVs with 4 MiB extents ≈ 25,598 extents (some space used for metadata). An LV of 10 GiB = 2,560 extents.

steps.title: Leave free space
steps.body: Keep some VG space free for snapshots and emergencies.

steps.title: Why

scenes.text: Ravi, a Java developer, opens main.dart and writes `String name = 'Asha';`. It works, but his teammate says 'we usually write final here'.

steps.title: var, final, const
steps.body:
- **var** lets the compiler infer the type; the variable can be reassigned (but not to a different type).
- **final** is assigned once at runtime and never again.
- **const** is a compile-time constant: the value must be known when the program is compiled.

`final now = DateTime.now();` is legal (known only at runtime). `const now = DateTime.now();` is a compile error.

steps.title: Read this code
Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking final means the object is immutable: a final List can still have items added; only the variable cannot be reassigned.
- Using const for values computed at runtime.
- Using `dynamic` to escape the type checker: you lose compile-time safety.

steps.title: Operators
steps.body:
- `/` always gives a **double**: `7 / 2` is `3.5`.
- `~/` is integer division: `7 ~/ 2` is `3`.
- `%` is remainder: `7 % 2` is `1`.
- Strings: `'Hi $name'` and `'Total ${a + b}'` use interpolation. Triple quotes `'''` make multi-line strings.

steps.title: Trace it

```dart
int a = 17;
int b = 5;
print(a ~/ b);   // 3
print(a % b);    // 2
print(a / b);    // 3.4
print('a=$a, sum=${a + b}'); // a=17, sum=22
```

steps.title: Type facts
steps.body: `int` and `double` are both subtypes of `num`. `int x = 5.0;` is an error, while `double y = 5;` is allowed in current Dart because integer literals can be used where a double is expected.

steps.title: Frame budget
steps.body: Frame time budget = 1000 ms divided by the refresh rate. At 60 Hz that is about 16.7 ms per frame; at 90 Hz about 11.1 ms; at 120 Hz about 8.3 ms. If the work for a frame (build, layout, paint, GPU raster) exceeds the budget, a frame is dropped: this is **jank**.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body:
1000 / 60 = 16.67 ms. 1000 / 120 = 8.33 ms.
A frame taking 12 ms is fine at 60 Hz but janky at 120 Hz.

scenes.text: Ananya from HR says the intranet page 'does not load'. Her colleague says 'the network is down'. Dev, the junior engineer, asks one question: does the page fail for everyone, or only for her?
That question is a layer question. Cable, address, route, port, or application all fail differently, and a layered model is how engineers avoid guessing.

steps.title: Why layers exist
steps.body:
A **layer** hides complexity: each layer offers a service to the layer above and uses the service below. Changing Wi-Fi to fibre does not force a rewrite of your web browser.

- **Interoperability**: vendors implement the same layer interface.
- **Troubleshooting**: you can test one layer at a time.
- **Teaching**: a shared vocabulary ('that is a Layer 2 problem').

steps.title: The seven OSI layers (top to bottom)
steps.body:
7 **Application** - network services to apps (HTTP, DNS, SMTP)
6 **Presentation** - encoding, compression, encryption format (TLS is often placed here or at 5)
5 **Session** - starts, manages and ends dialogues
4 **Transport** - end-to-end delivery, ports, TCP/UDP
3 **Network** - logical addressing and routing (IP)
2 **Data Link** - framing, MAC addressing, local delivery (Ethernet, Wi-Fi)
1 **Physical** - bits as signals on copper, fibre or radio

steps.title: The TCP/IP model
steps.body: TCP/IP has four layers: **Application** (OSI 5-7), **Transport** (4), **Internet** (3) and **Network Access / Link** (1-2). Many textbooks also show a five-layer hybrid that splits Link into Data Link and Physical. The real protocols follow TCP/IP; OSI is the reference vocabulary.

steps.title: PDU names
steps.body: The **protocol data unit** is called *data* at the upper layers, **segment** (TCP) or **datagram** (UDP) at Layer 4, **packet** at Layer 3, **frame** at Layer 2 and **bits** at Layer 1.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying 'a router works at Layer 2'. Routers forward on Layer 3 but have Layer 2 interfaces too.
- Treating OSI as the protocol stack in use. The Internet runs TCP/IP.
- Mixing 'packet' and 'frame': a frame wraps a packet.

steps.title: CIDR notation
steps.body: A prefix such as **/26** says the first 26 bits are network bits, so the mask is 255.255.255.192 and 6 host bits remain.

steps.title: MAC address
steps.body: A **MAC address** is 48 bits written as 6 hex pairs (e.g. 00:1A:2B:3C:4D:5E). The first 24 bits are the OUI (vendor); the rest identifies the interface. It is used only on the local segment.

steps.title: Ethernet frame
steps.body: Destination MAC (6) + Source MAC (6) + EtherType (2) + payload (46-1500) + FCS (4). The minimum frame is 64 bytes, the standard payload MTU is 1500.

steps.title: ARP
steps.body: **ARP** maps an IPv4 address to a MAC address on the same subnet: broadcast request (ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff), unicast reply. Replies are cached in the ARP table for minutes.

steps.title: Security note
steps.body: ARP has no authentication, so ARP spoofing is possible; switches can defend with Dynamic ARP Inspection.

steps.title: Mistake
steps.body: Thinking ARP crosses routers. It does not; you ARP for the gateway, never for a remote host.

steps.title: NAT
steps.body: **Network Address Translation** rewrites IP addresses (and with PAT, ports) as packets cross a border. It conserves public IPv4 addresses and hides internal addressing - but it is **not a firewall** and breaks end-to-end transparency.

steps.title: Terms
steps.body: **Inside local**: the inside host's private address. **Inside global**: how the inside host appears outside. **Outside global**: the outside host's real address. **Outside local**: how the outside host appears inside (usually the same as outside global).

steps.title: Types
steps.body: **Static NAT**: one-to-one fixed mapping (publish a server). **Dynamic NAT**: pool of public addresses, first come first served. **PAT / overload**: many inside hosts share one address distinguished by source port.

steps.title: Mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting `ip nat inside` / `ip nat outside` on interfaces.
- ACL for NAT that does not match the inside subnet.
- Treating NAT as security.

steps.title: ACL rules
steps.body: ACLs are processed **top-down, first match wins**; there is an **implicit deny any** at the end. Standard ACLs (1-99, 1300-1999) match source IP only; extended ACLs (100-199, 2000-2699) match protocol, source, destination and ports. Named ACLs allow editing by sequence numbers.

steps.title: Wildcard masks
steps.body: A **0 bit means must match**, **1 means ignore**. /24 -> 0.0.0.255; host -> 0.0.0.0 (or the `host` keyword); any -> 255.255.255.255 (`any`).

steps.title: Placement
steps.body: Put **extended** ACLs close to the **source** (stop unwanted traffic early); put **standard** ACLs close to the **destination** (they only see the source, so applying them near the source could block too much).

steps.title: Mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting `permit ip any any` before the implicit deny.
- Applying in the wrong direction.
- Wrong order: a broad permit above a specific deny.

lessons.title: Loops, broadcast storms and the STP election

scenes.text: Someone plugs a patch cable between two wall ports on the same switch. Within seconds the floor goes dead: CPU 99%, link LEDs blinking in sync.
Your turn: read the key ideas, then apply them hands-on in the activity that follows.

steps.title: Why
steps.body: Ethernet frames have no TTL. A looped broadcast is copied forever -> **broadcast storm**, MAC table instability, multiple frame copies.

steps.title: STP
steps.body: Spanning Tree Protocol (802.1D) builds a loop-free tree: elect one **root bridge** (lowest Bridge ID = priority + MAC), each non-root picks one **root port** (lowest path cost to root), each segment gets one **designated port**; the rest are **blocking**.

steps.title: Bridge ID

steps.title: Link-state
steps.body: Each router floods **LSAs** describing its links; all routers in an area build the same **LSDB** and run Dijkstra's SPF to compute shortest paths. Metric = **cost** = reference bandwidth / interface bandwidth (default reference 100 Mbps).

steps.title: Neighbour states
steps.body: Down -> Init -> 2-Way -> ExStart -> Exchange -> Loading -> **Full**. On broadcast networks a **DR** and **BDR** are elected (highest priority, then highest router ID; priority 0 = ineligible); other routers reach Full only with the DR/BDR and stay 2-Way with each other.

steps.title: Facts
steps.body: OSPF runs directly over IP protocol 89, multicast 224.0.0.5 (all OSPF routers) and 224.0.0.6 (DR/BDR). Hello/Dead timers: 10/40 s on broadcast and point-to-point.

steps.title: Neighbour must-match
steps.body: Area, hello/dead timers, subnet and mask, authentication, stub flag, and MTU (for adjacency to reach Full) - a unique router ID is also required.

steps.title: FHRP
